title: The good question
hook: in the study hall a sharp question earns more respect than a quick answer

segments.voice: Yesterday, chavruta: two people, one book, arguing out loud as friends. Your line was learn with a partner.

Other kids came home from school, the story goes, and their mothers asked: what did you learn today? Isidor Rabi's mother asked something else. Izzy, did you ask a good question today? Rabi grew up in a Jewish immigrant family in New York and became a Nobel Prize-winning physicist. He said that question made him a scientist. People often tell this story, and whether every detail happened just that way, nobody can check. It keeps getting retold because it fits the study hall so well. There, the person everyone turns to isn't the one with the fastest answer. It's the one who says: wait. That doesn't make sense.
screen: `WHAT DID YOU LEARN TODAY?` → `DID YOU ASK A GOOD QUESTION?` → `WAIT. THAT DOESN'T MAKE SENSE.`

segments.voice: Open the Mishnah, the early rabbinic collection of Jewish law, to its very first line. It doesn't start with a rule. It starts with a question: from what time may the Shema be said in the evening? The whole Talmud grows from there, and page after page, its engine is the question. The Aramaic word is kushya, a difficulty. A student notices two verses that seem to disagree, or a rule that doesn't fit, and says so. The Talmud doesn't hide these. It lines them up and works on them, sometimes for pages. Sometimes the answer never comes, and the Talmud says so plainly: teiku, let it stand. Some later readers heard in that word a hope that Elijah the prophet would one day come and settle it. Until then, the question stays on the table, honored. The rabbis also taught, in Pirkei Avot, that a shy person can't learn: someone too embarrassed to ask stays where they are. And every year at the Passover seder, a child, often the youngest, asks: why is this night different from all other nights? The Haggadah tells the story of the Exodus as an answer to a child's question. So what makes a question good? It's real: you actually want to know. It's close to the text: it points at a word, not a vague feeling. And it's brave: it risks sounding like you missed something. A quick answer ends the conversation. A good question starts it.
screen: `THE MISHNAH OPENS WITH A QUESTION.` · `KUSHYA: A DIFFICULTY, SAID OUT LOUD.` · `TEIKU: LET IT STAND.` · `A SHY PERSON CAN'T LEARN.` · then, large: `ASK BETTER.`

segments.voice: Think of something you've been told so often you stopped asking about it: a rule at work, a family habit, a line you've heard all your life. Ask one honest question about it, not a complaint, but a question you'd actually like answered. Turn it until it's sharp and short.
Kushya. A difficulty: the Aramaic word for the hard question that, in the study hall, earns more respect than a quick answer.
Your line: ask better. In the study hall, the hard question is the honored one. Day one hundred fifty-two, done.

howItsDone: In Jewish study, students are expected to raise difficulties with the text out loud, and the Talmud records unresolved questions rather than hiding them; at the Passover seder, children ask the Four Questions.

original.note: Aramaic: a difficulty, the hard question the Talmud raises and works on.

trapdoor: what you thought: a good question is one that has an easy answer.
what it means: a real, precise, brave question about the text, which in the study hall earns more respect than a quick reply.
what a scholar hears: Mishnah Berakhot 1:1 opens 'me'eimatai', from when; the Talmud's kushya and teiku; Avot 2:5, 'lo habayshan lamed', the bashful does not learn.

notes: The I. I. Rabi anecdote is widely retold (e.g. in a 1988 letter/interview); the script frames it as a story people tell and says the details can't be checked. Confirm the framing.
